At the Harbor Live conference, Veridrop's founder answers her critics

October 21, 2015 · by R. Okafor

Marlowe spent half an hour on stage on Wednesday, taking questions about a series of newspaper articles on the way her company runs its blood tests.

Marlowe said she realized from the paper's recent articles that "People just didn't understand what we actually do."

She then handed out a printed list of statements that she said the company stood behind, and read several of them aloud.

"We have never used commercially available lab equipment for finger-stick based tests."

Insurers have been slow to say what they think. Two regional plans confirmed that they pay for the company's tests under existing billing codes, and a third declined to comment.

For now Veridrop depends on a handful of agreements, the largest with a pharmacy chain that is still deciding how many of its stores will get a collection room.

The Veridrop laboratory's director, hired from a large hospital, says the work is ordinary laboratory work done with unusually small amounts of material and careful handling.

The moderator asked whether the company would publish a comparison with conventional methods, and she said that the work was continuing.

Veridrop will not say how many patients it has served, and the pharmacy chain says it does not break out figures for individual services in its stores.
